newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany agrees investment plan for struggling east.
newsitem.headline: Germany agrees investment plan for struggling east.

text.p: Germany agreed to a new investment support package on Wednesday for the former communist east, still a jobs and economic blackspot seven years and more than a trillion marks of state aid after unification in 1990.

Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said the plan would initially keep investment support for east Germany at constant levels but would cost around half as much by scrapping generous tax write-offs now available to investors in the region.

The total burden on Germany's annual budget, already stretching to meet single European currency entry criteria, will fall from a current 11 billion marks to 5.7 billion marks in 1999 and then to 4.4 billion after 2002.

The package comes before a separate plan for a "jobs pact" Bonn will launch on Thursday with trade unions and business to create 100,000 jobs a year in a region where unemployment is stuck at 17 percent, rising to 25 percent in some towns.

Rexrodt said the new package would from next year offer specifically-targeted investment grants rather than the existing tax depreciation incentives that have in the past led to investments often seen as having dubious value.

He added the emphasis would shift towards promoting commercial and industrial activity rather than the continued building of new offices and apartments in a regional market which is already suffering from chronic oversupply.

The new investment package will come in next year at the same time as a promised cut in the solidarity tax surcharge which has helped finance much of the reconstruction of east Germany but is becoming increasingly unpopular among west Germans who pay the lion's share of it.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl, anxious to bolster east Germans' faith in a government which promised them an economy with "blossoming landscapes" after unification, will himself present the new jobs pact in Berlin on Thursday.

In what would be strikingly similar to the failed "Alliance for Jobs" that collapsed amid acrimony between trade unions and the government just over a year ago, the new jobs plan is widely expected to link job creation to reduced labour costs.

Opposition Social Democrat (SPD) politicians welcomed the employment plan ahead of its formal announcement but SPD parliamentary economics spokesman Ernst Schwanhold said the delay in bringing in such a measure "had destroyed thousands of jobs" in the meantime.
East German politicians approved the new investment plan, particularly the move to replace depreciation allowances with direct grants.

"Now it's up to businesses to use the investment incentives. We urge and encourage them to do so," said Joachim Schmidt, chairman of the state of Saxony parliamentary grouping within Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU).
